newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia sells 49 pct telecom to Stet, OTE.
newsitem.headline: Serbia sells 49 pct telecom to Stet, OTE.

text.p: Serbian post and telecommunications company PTT sold on Monday a 49 precent stake in its telecom department to Stet of Italy and OTE of Greece in a deal worth close to $1 billion.
"The deal was signed as we planned. We got 1.568 billion German marks ($909.7 million) for 49 percent stake of Serbian telecom," Dragan Peric, Serbian PTT's deputy general manager told Reuters.
Stet bought 29 percent stake for 893 million German marks and OTE paid 675 million German marks to acquire a 20 percent stake in the Telekom Srbija.
The total value of the Serbian telecommunications was estimated at 3.2 billion German marks.
Serbia will preserve control over its most lucrative sector by retaining a 51 percent stake in its telecom company.
"Stet and OTE acted independently and we have signed a tripartite deal. There have been no diplomatic pressures to halt the deal," Serbian privatisation minister Milan Beko told a news conference.
He was referring to unofficial reports that the United States had moved to block the deal in its early stages.

Washington has maintained an outer wall of sanctions barring Belgrade from foreign funds in the hope the lack of cash would force Milosevic to cooperate with a war crimes tribunal and improve human rights in his troubled mainly-Albanian populated province of Kosovo.
But West European states have rebuffed Washington, because, in the words of a senior European diplomat, this was an "American policy matter and no concern of ours".

"This represents a positive fact and gives hope for the development of even more useful relations in line with the best interests of the citizens of both countries," Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told his Yugoslav counter-part Milan Milutinovic in a letter on Monday on the ocassion of the deal.
"By signing this deal, Serbia confirmed its place on an international investment map as an important target for foreign capital inflow," he said.
Beko insisted funds raised through the sale of 49 percent stake in its vital national utility would be directed to the Serbian state development fund.
"Money raised from a sale of public companies... will be exclusively used to support development and export-oriented programmes," he added.
The minister said the government did not go for an open tender, opting instead for biggest world telecom operators.
"Our intention was to find a strategic partner to help us join international alliances and technological integrations," Beko said.

PTT Srbije managing director Aleksa Jokic said Telekom Srbija was granted a right to exploit fixed and mobile telephony over next 20 years. Joint exploitation, including rights for Stet and OTE, is planned for the first eight years.
"With this agreement, we have obtained another mobile phones operator in Serbia," Jokic said.

According to the agreement Telekom Srbija will pay a two percent licence fee -- two percent of annual revenues equalling around 20 million German marks -- to PTT Srbije for the right to operate as a telecom operator in the country.

In the first year of its operations, Telekom Srbija will pay a total of 135 million German marks to PTT Srbije for the lease of its premises and purchase of some services -- data processing, collecting phone bills, etc.
Telekom Srbije will pay 125 million marks as a licence fee for the second year. The sum will be reduced over the years but will never go below 50 million German marks a year.

PTT Srbije will use those funds to upgrade the postal system, to allow a complete separation of postal and telecommunications units within the company and enable the Serbian post to become profitable, Jokic said.
Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic welcomed the deal signed with the Italian and Greek companies.

"The most important thing is to push the process forward. This is the fastest way to get going with fresh funds. We are forced to sell some of our family silver because we are squeezed from all sides," Djunic told Reuters.

"Everybody expects us to go on with reforms, to keep stability, but we need money for that. We have been forced to sell because we have no manoeuvring space," he added. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
